articles.title: Malaysia shuts schools as haze from Indonesian fires chokes Southeast Asia
articles.summary: Kuala Lumpur’s Air Pollutant Index says air quality at unhealthy levels amid smog from forest fires.
articles.body:
Malaysia has closed schools in its capital and several states as smoke from Indonesian forest fires pushes air pollution to unhealthy levels.

Schools were ordered to close on Friday across Kuala Lumpur, the administrative capital Putrajaya and in the states of Johor, Malacca, Negeri Sembilan, Pahang and Selangor.

The move, which affected roughly two million students, came as Kuala Lumpur recorded an Air Pollutant Index (API) reading of about 170. The API is a government-run measure of air quality.

Singapore, at the southern end of the Malay Peninsula, saw its air quality fall into the “very unhealthy” range, according to IQAir.

“The haze issue is indeed at a worrying level,” said Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim. He added that he had spoken to Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto, who had agreed to take “the necessary steps”. However, he offered no details on what that might entail.

Anwar said he had asked Malaysia’s minister of foreign affairs to push for an urgent meeting of ASEAN environment ministers. Kuala Lumpur is stepping up cloud seeding to trigger rain, he added.

“Appropriate measures must be taken by the relevant ministries and agencies to protect schoolchildren and students, including senior citizens and patients with respiratory illnesses,” King Sultan Ibrahim said. He declared that schools should close when API readings hit 150 or higher.

Under Malaysian guidelines, API readings above 100 are classified as unhealthy, above 200 as very unhealthy, above 300 as hazardous, while readings beyond 500 constitute the threshold for declaring a local emergency.

Education Minister Fadhlina Sidek promised parents more advance notice of closures in future.

In August, Indonesia’s coordinating minister for political and security affairs said that El Nino conditions were threatening more fires during the dry season.

A month later, smoke started to blanket the region as the country experienced its worst fire season in over a decade.

Fires have burned across six provinces, with at least 200,000 hectares scorched, Al Jazeera’s Jessica Washington reported.

Indonesia’s Ministry of Health has recorded more than 170,000 respiratory infections, but the actual figure is likely higher as it only covers those who sought out healthcare, she noted.

The haze has also worried organisers of Singapore’s Formula One weekend, which is set to start on Friday and end on Sunday.

Organisers have insisted that they will race regardless and will have masks and extra medics, adding that it is “not a threat”.

articles.title: Ukraine takes aim at Russia’s AI data infrastructure
articles.summary: Drone attacks target Russian digital giant Yandex, as well as continuing strikes on missile plants and oil refineries.
articles.body:
Ukrainian drone strikes have partly disabled an AI data centre operated by Russian digital giant Yandex.

The strike on Friday followed an attack on another of the company’s data hubs the previous day, appearing to signal that Ukraine’s military campaign is widening its scope to target Russia’s technology infrastructure. Moscow has previously targeted data hubs inside Ukraine.

Yandex, which is heavily involved in Russia’s AI development efforts, said its data centre in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow had been struck by Ukrainian drones and partly put out of action.

A day earlier, a Ukrainian attack shut down a major data hub in Sasovo in the Ryazan region, where two of the three supercomputers used to develop the company’s AI models are housed.

Yandex, which operates under close government observation, said the attacks had struck at the core of its operations and that it was trying to maintain its services.

“Our teams are working day and night to keep services running and help those affected by the incident. Right now this is our most important task, but unfortunately it is not an easy one,” it said in a statement.

The company operates numerous apps that many Russians consider essential, as well as social media networks.

Russia has struck several Ukrainian data centres and telecommunications infrastructure facilities over the past month, including targets in central Kyiv.

Damage from the attacks has forced some services to suspend operations. Roughly 100,000 households suffered temporary internet outages after an attack.

“We always respond in mirror-like fashion,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday, following the Ryazan strike. “You all know, they have been hitting and continue to hit our data centres. We are responding. I can’t share all the details.”

Kyiv also continues its campaign targeting Russia’s missile production and energy infrastructure, hoping to reduce the air strikes against which it has struggled to defend, as well as to hurt Moscow’s economic ability to wage war.

Ukraine’s military said it had hit three facilities involved in missile production across Russia overnight, including a factory in the Tver region making missile components and a centre for disassembling intercontinental ballistic missiles in the Nizhny Novgorod region.

In a statement on Telegram, the General Staff said the Russian facility for the “liquidation of intercontinental ballistic missiles” was hit to degrade Russia’s ability to source explosives and rocket fuel.

Nizhny Novgorod’s governor said that one serviceman was killed repelling the attack while drone debris caused “minimal” damage to infrastructure.

A drone attack sparked a fire at a plant in Redkino in the Tver region, but it was quickly extinguished, the local governor said.

The Ukhta oil refinery belonging to the state giant Lukoil, 1,900km (1,180 miles) from the Ukrainian border, was also struck, according to Zelenskyy.

Meanwhile, Russia’s air campaign has continued to hit civilians, despite the Kremlin’s insistence that it only attacks military targets.

Overnight strikes killed one and injured seven in the city of Zaporizhzhia, regional defence official Ivan Fedorov said on the Telegram messaging app.

Russia also struck a cargo vessel in Ukraine’s Black Sea port of Mykolaiv, the Ministry of Defence in Moscow said, according to state news agency RIA Novosti. The ministry said the vessel was being used to supply the Ukrainian military.

articles.title: Ukraine pushes Russia back in Donetsk as military, civilian casualties soar
articles.summary: Russia is fighting for settlements it once firmly held in Donetsk, and has retreated from many others.
articles.body:
Russian forces continue to retreat in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region.

The Kremlin-aligned channel Rybar, on Telegram, said on October 7 that Moscow’s forces were losing villages south of Lyman, a town they have tried to capture as a springboard to mount a full-scale offensive on the “fortress belt” cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.

A Ukrainian counteroffensive named “Operation Vivaldi” this year has reclaimed 175 square kilometres (67 square miles) of previously occupied land around Lyman.

“The enemy is using successes in the Lyman direction to develop attacks [east of Sloviansk], where Russian troops are forced to defend previously occupied positions and expend resources on restoring control, instead of launching their own offensive,” wrote Rybar.

“It is becoming increasingly clear that the possibility of storming the urban area [of Sloviansk] is receding into the more distant future.”

A key battle seems to be building for the village of Kryva Luka east of Sloviansk, which sits on high ground on the Russian-held right bank of the Siversky-Donets River, and which could serve as a base to launch counterattacks further east.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Reuters news agency that Operation Vivaldi was successful but incomplete.

To get as far as Kryva Luka, Russian sources acknowledged that Ukraine has recaptured settlements west of it. They blamed the Russian communications strategy of claiming settlements that have not been captured, giving away the plan of attack.

“Premature statements” aided Ukraine, said Rybar. “Some villages were declared liberated even before Russian units arrived, which allowed the enemy to accumulate forces there and launch counterattacks.”

Ukraine built up reserves in the Lyman area before unfolding its counteroffensive. That preparation seems to be yielding results.

Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence said its campaign to disrupt the flow of Russian ammunition and fuel to the front struck a record number of air defence assets and targets more than 50km (30 miles) away in September.

Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed Russia had captured 1,300sq km (500sq miles) of Ukraine in September, echoing claims by his generals.

The Institute for the Study of War, which monitors territorial advances using geolocated, open-source data, said Russia actually lost 80sq km (30sq miles) during that month.

The Russian casualty rate rose to a record for 2026 of 46,230 in September , according to Ukraine’s military.

Of these, 33,087 – more than 70 percent – were confirmed kills, said Ukraine.

The commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, Robert Brovdi, said enemy casualties were up by 40 percent in the first five days of October, compared with the same period in September.

The Ukrainian military on October 7 counted 1,545,950 Russian dead and wounded for the entire full-scale invasion since 2022.

Putin’s response has been to intensify bombing, causing civilian suffering.

Twenty-two people, five of them children, were killed in the city of Pryluky, in the northern Chernihiv region, when a Russian cruise missile demolished a five-storey apartment building on October 7, Putin’s birthday.

“Today, for Putin’s birthday, the Russian army ‘gifted’ the destruction of a residential building in Pryluky,” said Zelenskyy.

Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia unleashed 130 drones and 48 cruise missiles across 12 regions that day, as well as ballistics. At least two more people died in Kyiv and two in Oleksandria.

At least 30 people died in Kramatorsk on October 8, when a Russian bomb struck two city buses. Video of the emergency response showed bodies strewn across an avenue and in a park.

Recent analysis of the Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones Russia increasingly uses for many of its attacks makes it unlikely that these attacks on nonmilitary targets are accidental.

Ukraine’s military intelligence said the attacks use satellite and sophisticated inertial navigation systems, as well as a camera that reads landmark features and checks them against an on-board database – all three systems working in concert to ensure accurate navigation.

Ukraine has responded to the jet-powered drones by speeding up delivery of F-16 fighters from its allies, which are proving an effective first line of defence.

“Currently, F-16s are destroying between 50 percent and 60 percent of the drone attacks,” said Zelenskyy.

Ukraine is also testing five new types of interceptor drones, the most successful of which is 30 percent effective, and experimenting with small-scale missiles, Zelenskyy said.

A dozen AI-driven heavy machine-gun turrets have been placed around Kyiv as a last line of defence, with dozens more planned around the country.

These are a “facility-level” defence, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, a senior Defence Ministry adviser. “It can protect a warehouse, factory, bridge, or power substation.”

Russia has begun hitting bridges across the Dnipro River, striking Kyiv’s southern and northern bridges seven times in the first four days of October. It has previously struck the building where Ukraine’s cabinet met, as well as energy facilities feeding the city, in an effort to cause a blackout.

Russia’s jet-powered drones travel at more than 500km (310 miles) per hour and are more difficult to intercept than its propeller-driven Shahed drones.

Despite this, during the October 7 strike, Ukraine’s Air Force said it intercepted 80 percent of the jet-powered drones, 95 percent of the propeller-driven drones and 80 percent of cruise missiles.

On October 7, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Kyiv to announce a 1.3-billion-euro ($1.46bn) military aid package, and to sign agreements worth 8.5 billion euros ($9.5bn) to jointly develop drone defences and other weapons with Ukraine.

Merz’s visit was an important political gesture following recent elections in two German states where the pro-Russian AfD trounced his governing CDU party.

Ukraine continued long-range strikes inside Russia.

These struck refineries in Volgograd on October 2 and Bashkortostan on October 8, as part of a strategy to starve the Russian economy and military of fuel.

“Over 51 percent of the enemy’s oil refining capacity has been disabled,” said Ukraine’s military.

Ukraine also hit the Samara linear production and dispatch station, which its General Staff described as “a major hub for receiving, storing, and blending oil”.

The staff said eleven 20,000-tonne storage tanks and three 50,000-tonne storage tanks had been destroyed.

“The facility blends high- and low-sulfur oil from various fields to produce the export grade of oil known as Urals, which accounts for up to 50 percent of the total volume of Russian oil exports,” the military said.

Ukraine also struck military targets. On October 7, it struck the Astrakhan Gas Processing Plant, which extracts gaseous sulphur for use in explosives.

On October 4, it destroyed a Sukhoi Su-35 multi-role fighter and a Sukhoi Su-34 fighter-bomber on the Adygea airfield, and also hit the Seshcha airfield in Bryansk.

Its campaign of mid-range strikes to destroy Russian power supply in occupied areas had reached 456 between July 6 and October 3.

articles.title: Two men deny Iran-backed surveillance of Jewish and Israeli sites in London
articles.summary: Targets allegedly included the Israeli embassy and consulate, a woman said to be of interest to Iran, a college, and Britain's oldest synagogue.
articles.body:
Two men have pleaded not guilty to carrying out surveillance on Jewish and Israeli sites across London on behalf of Iran's intelligence service.

Nematollah Shahsavani, 41, and Alireza Farasati, 22, are accused of engaging in conduct likely to assist a foreign intelligence service under the National Security Act 2023.

Prosecutors allege the pair carried out hostile reconnaissance at several locations between 9 July and 15 August last year.

Targets allegedly included the Israeli embassy and consulate, a woman said to be of interest to Iran, a college, and Britain's oldest synagogue.

Both defendants entered their not not guilty pleas during an appearance at the Old Bailey on Friday. Farasati appeared in person in the dock, while Shahsavani attended via video link from HMP Pentonville.

The court previously heard that police confiscated electronic devices from Farasati, a barber, when he was stopped on 14 August last year.

Prosecutors allege that Shahsavani directed Farasati to monitor and gather intelligence on London's Jewish and Israeli communities. Shahsavani, who works as a car salesman and delivery driver, was allegedly acting on instructions from Iranian intelligence.

Shahsavani, a dual British-Iranian national and father of two from North Finchley, north London, has lived in the UK since 2009.

Farasati, an Iranian national living in Colindale, north-west London, arrived in Britain as a 17-year-old in 2021.

Mrs Judge Cheema-Grubb scheduled a further pre-trial hearing for 12 February, with a full trial due to begin at the Old Bailey on 26 April next year.

Both men, who were detained in March, remain in custody.

articles.title: Wakefield man who kept wife's body in freezer jailed for life
articles.summary: David Barraclough is jailed for at least 22 years for killing Carolann Barraclough.
articles.body:
A man who murdered his wife with a hammer and hid her body in a chest freezer while telling family and friends she was ill in hospital has been jailed for life.

David Barraclough, 46, killed Carolann Barraclough, a mother of three, at the family's house in Horbury, near Wakefield, in February.

Leeds Crown Court heard he then spent about two weeks trying to conceal what he had done, telling relatives and friends she was in hospital and sending messages from her phone pretending to be her.

Barraclough pleaded guilty to murder on the first day of his trial and refused to attend court for sentencing. He was jailed for life with a minimum term of 22 years and one month.

The court heard Carolann Barraclough was killed sometime between 19 and 21 February.

After her death, Barraclough tied up her body and placed it in a freezer in the utility room of the home they shared.

Prosecutors said he repeatedly lied to her children, family, friends and neighbours, claiming she was in hospital recovering from an illness and that only he was able to visit her.

He also used her phone to send messages suggesting she would soon return home and prevented the children from entering the room where the freezer was kept.

On 5 March, Barraclough walked into Normanton Police Station and told a receptionist: "I've killed my wife."

Officers who went to the family home found Carolann Barraclough's body inside the freezer.

The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said evidence showed Barraclough continued with his daily life after the killing, including visiting pubs, withdrawing large sums of cash from a joint bank account and downloading the dating app Tinder two days after his wife's death.

He later claimed he had acted in self-defence after being struck with a hammer and described himself as "heartbroken", "in a haze" and "confused".

However, prosecutors said CCTV footage showed no visible injuries and rejected his account.

Jill May, senior crown prosecutor for CPS Yorkshire and Humberside, said: "After brutally murdering Carolann, Barraclough hid her body in the home she shared with her children and lied repeatedly to her friends and family as he spun a calculated web of lies, pretending she was alive and recovering from illness in hospital."

She praised Carolann Barraclough's eldest daughter for her "incredible bravery" in providing evidence.

In a statement read to the court, Carolann Barraclough's family said she had been "the bright light of our family" whose "joy was infectious".

They said: "Caz was a vital and irreplaceable part of our family. The world is a much darker place without her."

A separate statement on behalf of her three children said all were autistic and had relied heavily on routine, familiarity and knowing the adults around them would keep them safe.

It said: "For two weeks they were told their mum was in hospital, but their mum was in their own home."

The statement added the children had lost "their world, their security and the future they were supposed to have with their mum".

Listen to highlights from West Yorkshire on BBC Sounds , catch up with the latest episode of Look North .

articles.title: Ethiopia and Eritrea accuse one another of launching war
articles.summary: Eritrea denies backing TPLF as Ethiopia alleges collusion, further straining their already volatile relationship.
articles.body:
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of an “all-out invasion” in a message to the United Nations Security Council, while Eritrea says it is facing a “war of aggression” from its neighbour.

“The all-out invasion of parts of northern Ethiopia by Eritrea is a matter of public record,” said a letter by Ethiopia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Gedion Timothewos, which was shared with news agencies on Friday.

“It is a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence,” added the letter dated Thursday and addressed to French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot.

Gedion said that Eritrean troops had advanced up to 60 kilometres (37 miles) into Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region and demanded their withdrawal, just days after the two nations cut diplomatic ties.

Eritrea’s Minister of Information Yemane Gebremeskel rejected Ethiopia’s claims.

“The Ethiopian regime has been pursuing, in effect, an unprovoked war of aggression against Eritrea for more than three years now,” he said on X.

Yemane said Asmara had shown restraint since landlocked Ethiopia had essentially declared a war against Eritrea when it stated in 2023 that it would gain access to the sea.

Citing statements made by Ethiopian officials, Yemane accused Addis Ababa of using the current conflict ⁠to take Assab, an Eritrean port, in order to restore access to the Red Sea.

Eritrea also denied Ethiopia’s claim that it is backing the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which is part of an alliance of seven armed groups that has been attempting to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government since September.

Over the past week, Ethiopia’s army has pushed back the TPLF and seized the Tigrayan capital, Mekelle.

Witnesses also told the AFP news agency that rebels had lost the Tigrayan cities of Shire and Adigrat. Eritrean troops were reportedly seen in Adigrat before Ethiopian drone strikes hit them, according to several witnesses.

Ethiopia and Eritrea have traded accusations since the reported ⁠incursions by Eritrean troops this week raised fears of outright war in the region, where the two nations have fought previous conflicts.

The stakes have been raised this time around by conflicts in the Horn of Africa region and tensions across the Red Sea.

Diplomatic ties between the two have collapsed amid the escalation: Ethiopia closed its embassy in Asmara and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave the country last week. In response, Eritrea announced it was severing ties.

The neighbours have a tumultuous history, as Eritrea won independence from Ethiopia in 1993 and they fought a border war for two years in 1998.

Relations improved slightly in 2018 when Abiy took power in Addis Ababa, and Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopia against the TPLF in a civil war from 2020 to 2022.

Eritrea, however, was not part of the peace deal that ended the war, which soured ties soon afterwards.

Tensions are also fuelled by Abiy’s repeated claim that landlocked Ethiopia – which lost its access to the coast when Eritrea secured independence – has a right to sea access , which Eritrea sees as a threat to seize its Red Sea port of Assab.

articles.title: Empire State Building lights up red, white and blue to celebrate Fox News Channel's 30th anniversary
articles.summary: The Empire State Building glowed red, white and blue as the "FOX & Friends" co-hosts celebrated Fox News Channel's three decades in cable news.
articles.body: The New York City skyline was extra patriotic on Thursday night when the Empire State Building was lit up with red, white and blue in celebration of Fox News Channel's 30th anniversary. "FOX & Friends" co-hosts Steve Doocy, Ainsley Earhardt, Brian Kilmeade and Lawrence Jones gathered at the world-famous Empire State Building Observation Deck to help flip the switch and take a special tour of the landmark. "Since its launch in 1996, Fox News has grown from a new cable news network into an established presence in American television news. Over the past three decades, the network has covered some of the most consequential stories and events of our time, with generations of journalists, anchors, correspondents, producers and teams who have contributed to its 24-hour news coverage," Empire State Building GM Dan Rogoski said before inviting the "FOX & Friends" co-hosts to say a few words. LAUREN GREEN: I WAS FOX NEWS CHANNEL'S FIRST ON-AIR HIRE. HERE'S HOW A DREAM BECAME A POWERHOUSE Doocy, an original employee who was with the network when it launched on Oct. 7, 1996, thanked Fox Corporation Chairman Emeritus Rupert Murdoch, Fox Corp Executive Chair and Chief Executive Officer Lachlan Murdoch, FOX News Media CEO Suzanne Scott and FOX News Media President and Executive Editor Jay Wallace. "You know, as one of the original people at the Fox News Channel based here in Midtown, we are delighted that the Empire State Building would honor us," Doocy said. Earhardt discussed how fortunate the hosts are to come from "humble beginnings" and wind up flipping the switch to light up such an iconic building. "I love ‘Sleepless in Seattle,’ and I've never been up on the … I'm reminded of my 10-year-old self," Earhardt said. MIKE EMANUEL: I JOINED AN UNKNOWN STARTUP CALLED FOX NEWS; IT GAVE ME A FRONT-ROW SEAT TO HISTORY Kilmeade, who was battling laryngitis, joked that the building reminded him of a different movie, "Elf." He called Fox News a fantastic place that continues to evolve and allows on-air personalities to develop, be themselves and thrive. "They hire you to be you. Anyone on the air that you like or dislike, you will feel the same way when you meet them, because they're told to be that way and are allowed to be ourselves. It's one of the most fortunate things that could ever happen to me personally," Kilmeade said. "It's truly a thrill to be here. I know Fox would be successful without me, but I'm sure happy to be along for the ride," he continued. "Thanks so much. Also, special thanks to Rupert Murdoch, who is relentless and opened up the wallet to do it. Lachlan Murdoch is cut out of the same mold in every way, and Suzanne Scott … she goes into the Hall of Fame for a reason. Unbelievable under pressure, great adjustments to this new marketplace, and Jay Wallace, one of the great success stories at Fox. Started at the very bottom and now is at the top." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Indeed, Scott was inducted into the Broadcasting+Cable Hall of Fame last week, joining innovators, visionaries and leaders who have shaped the media landscape. Jones, who regularly says that Scott has been instrumental in his career, said it was a "dream come true" to be at the ceremony. "What Rupert Murdoch did 30 years ago is truly legendary. There was a void in the market. He understood that there was an audience that was untapped and felt like they were underserved. And his son, Lachlan Murdoch, is keeping that tradition going. Without Suzanne Scott, Jay Wallace giving me the opportunity of a lifetime 10 years ago, I would not be able to stand before y'all today and be in a building that I only used to see in movies," Jones said. articles.title: Margaret Hamilton, who led a software team for NASA’s Apollo program, dies at 90
articles.summary: Margaret Hamilton, a groundbreaking computer scientist who led the team that created the onboard flight software for NASA’s moon-bound Apollo program and later in life was celebrated as a powerful symbol of women in technology, has died.
articles.body: Margaret Hamilton, a groundbreaking computer scientist who led the team that created the onboard flight software for NASA’s moon-bound Apollo program and later in life was celebrated as a powerful symbol of women in technology, has died. She was 90. Hamilton died Sept. 30 at a hospital in Cambridge, Massachusetts, her daughter, Lauren Hamilton, told The Associated Press on Thursday. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on the social platform X that her work helped make humanity’s first journeys to the moon possible. “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” Olivier de Weck, the Apollo program professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and interim head of its aeronautics and astronautics department, told MIT News, a publication of the university’s communications office. “She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.” In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton. And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said. “She definitely went from nobody knowing who she was to suddenly everyone knowing who she was, especially in her field,” Lauren Hamilton said. “And I think she was really happy to be acknowledged for what she did. But she was kind of a reserved person so the spotlight wasn’t necessarily a natural thing for her.” Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959. Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT’s Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo. After first working on software for uncrewed missions, she later led the team developing the onboard flight software for the crewed missions, and by 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the command and service module team, according to MIT News. “We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. “Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure.” “Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust,” she continued. “We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.” She worked at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s and then founded two software companies, according to MIT News. Lauren Hamilton said her mother’s biggest interest was in the abstract. “She was very much a mathematician and into the abstraction of how to turn thought, I guess, into software,” she said. She said her mother was also “a really eccentric and fun character” who loved collecting vintage clothing and had “a very mischievous sense of humor.” “She encountered a lot of sexism in her field but she didn’t come back aggressively,” Lauren Hamilton said. “She would disarm people with her sense of humor or … just kind of dominate quietly.” Born on Aug. 17, 1936, in Indiana, Hamilton grew up mostly in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, her daughter said, and she lived in Cambridge from when she was in her early 20s until her death. Hamilton received many awards and accolades, including being awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor, in 2016 by President Barack Obama.

articles.title: Nightmare flight forced to divert to New York after 6 restrooms fail midair
articles.summary: After six of its eight lavatories failed, leaving only two working mid-flight, American Airlines Flight 37 from Madrid to Dallas diverted to JFK in New York City.
articles.body: A vacation nightmare recently unfolded on an international flight bound for Texas when six lavatories stopped working while the plane was in the air. American Airlines flight 37 was traveling from Madrid, Spain, to Dallas Fort Worth International Airport on Oct. 6 when it diverted to New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport due to the restroom fail. An American Airlines spokesperson confirmed the diversion to Fox News Digital, citing "an issue with the aircraft's lavatories." PROBE UNDERWAY AS 7 FLIGHT ATTENDANTS SICKENED BY BAFFLING ODOR ON MAJOR AIRLINE "On Oct. 6, American Airlines flight 37, with service from Madrid (MAD) to Dallas Fort Worth (DFW), diverted to New York (JFK) due to an issue with the aircraft's lavatories," the spokesperson said. Six of the aircraft's eight lavatories were not working — leaving only two available during the transatlantic flight, according to reports. The extent of the problem was also heard in communications between the cockpit and air traffic control by LiveATC.net, a website that streams air traffic control communications. When a controller asked why the aircraft needed to divert, the pilot reported that only two lavatories remained operational. articles.title: 'Jo aadmi darta hai': Kharge invokes 'Sholay' dialogue to target govt over Delhi curbs amid anti-CEC protests
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Friday invoked the iconic “Jo darr gaya” (one who gets scared) dialogue from the 1975 blockbuster
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Friday invoked the iconic “Jo darr gaya” (one who gets scared) dialogue from the 1975 blockbuster "Sholay" to target the government, as opposition parties continued their protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.Kharge was referring to the sweeping restrictions imposed by the Delhi Police ahead of Saturday’s planned protest by youth pressure group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and other student organisations, which are demanding the removal or resignation of Kumar.Speaking to reporters in the Parliament House complex ahead of the opposition’s march to Rashtrapati Bhavan to meet President Droupadi Murmu over the issue, Kharge remarked, “They (the government) are scared. ‘Aur jo aadmi darta hai vo aaj nahi toh kal marta hai’ (a person who is scared will die, if not today then tomorrow).”His remark was an apparent reference to the iconic dialogue delivered by dacoit Gabbar Singh, the main antagonist played by Amjad Khan in the film.Kharge also claimed that the two Election Commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had openly stated that CEC Kumar had made a “mistake”.“Both commissioners themselves said that we raised objections several times and explained to Gyanesh Kumar, but he did not agree. Despite the objections of the two election commissioners, the Modi government is not ready to remove Gyanesh Kumar from his post,” he added, referring to a media report that triggered the ongoing controversy.Describing Kumar as a “small fish”, Kharge alleged that he had the backing of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah.“Gyanesh Kumar is a small fish, but behind him are (Narendra) Modi-(Amit) Shah and their government. The Modi government wants all rights to be stripped away and dictatorship to be imposed. If dictatorship comes, democracy will end, which will also wipe out the Constitution and all rights. We are fighting for the sake of democracy, the constitution, and the people's interests,” Kharge stated.(With PTI inputs)Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: Convicted University of Idaho student murderer Bryan Kohberger is trying to remove the judge who called him a "faceless coward" and said he could find nothing "good or intrinsically human" about him at sentencing — but prosecutors say those remarks don't prove bias as the former criminology student fights to undo his guilty plea. Judge Steven Hippler said Kohberger, 31, "slithered" into the victims' home before committing a crime that made him "the worst of the worst" after the killer admitted guilt last year. He also addressed the lack of a requirement that he explain himself as part of a plea deal to avoid the death penalty. "Even if I could force him to speak, which legally I cannot, how could anyone ever be assured that what he speaks is the truth?" Hippler asked during sentencing. "Do we really believe, after all of this, he is capable of speaking the truth, or of giving up something of himself to help the very people whose lives he destroyed? Rather, I suspect the so-called reason would be dished out in enticing self-serving and aggrandizing untruthful bits, leaving people wanting more information, more insight, and thus enhancing even further the power he seeks to hold." BRYAN KOHBERGER'S BID TO OUST JUDGE AND UNDO GUILTY PLEA MOVES FORWARD WITH NEW COURT DATE SET The judge was also seen wiping tears from his eyes after hearing emotional victim impact statements. Kohberger's new legal team filed a motion seeking Hippler's removal on Aug. 27, arguing he had made biased statements during the convicted killer's sentencing and had rushed the case toward trial when their client's former defense team wasn't ready. IDAHO JUDGE GRANTS BRYAN KOHBERGER TWO HEARINGS NEXT YEAR AS ADMITTED KILLER SEEKS TO WITHDRAW GUILTY PLEA Prosecutors wrote that in order for a judge to be removed, "the motion must show that 'the judge is biased,'" italicizing the "is" for emphasis. "None of petitioner's allegations against this Court — taken alone or together — have [met] that 'extremely high' bar," reads a filing signed by outgoing Latah County Prosecuting Attorney Bill Thompson, who announced his retirement earlier this week, and Deputy Prosecuting Attorney Keith Scholl. IDAHO PROSECUTORS ACCUSE BRYAN KOHBERGER OF 'FISHING' TO FIND BETTER ARGUMENTS FOR BID TO WITHDRAW GUILTY PLEA Scholl had previously asked the court for the transcripts from Kohberger's change of plea and sentencing hearings, in which the former criminology Ph.D. student admitted guilt and affirmed he was entering his plea knowingly and under no duress. BRYAN KOHBERGER’S 2027 HEARING IS NOT GUARANTEED AS IDAHO SEEKS QUICK DISMISSAL The opposition filing argues that Hippler's statements about Kohberger after he'd admitted to killing four innocent students were not unusual or out of line. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X "In our case, the sentencing remarks are not enough to show bias, and the required showing of perceived bias cannot be tied to this Court's capacity to fairly adjudicate any [post-conviction relief] claims alleged in this case but rather puts this Court in the best position to adjudicate them as the legislature and the Idaho Supreme Court's rules intend," prosecutors wrote. BRYAN KOHBERGER'S NEW LAWYER SAYS KEY QUESTIONS MAY SOON GET ANSWERS IN COURT The court appointed attorney Greg Rauch, of Moscow, Idaho, to take over his case. articles.title: Nobel Peace Prize awarded to UN jurist who accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza
articles.summary: Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay chaired the UN commission that accused Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant of inciting genocide in Gaza.
articles.body: Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, an experienced jurist who chaired a United Nations commission that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for "her efforts to promote peace and international law." In awarding this year's Peace Prize, the Nobel Committee argued strong international judicial institutions must be able to enforce the rule of law to have any hope of mediating the growing number of wars and conflicts worldwide. The committee also noted that political attacks against judges and international law itself are becoming more commonplace. Pillay has had a long, storied career — both as a lawyer and as a judge — and more recently, she has definitively weighed in on the conflict between Israel and Hamas. ISRAEL ACCUSES UN OF PLACING IT ON SAME SEXUAL VIOLENCE BLACKLIST AS HAMAS TERRORISTS, SEVERS TIES She chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which was created in 2021 after a flare-up in tensions between Israelis and Palestinians. In September 2025, nearly two years after the Oct. 7 attacks, the commission concluded that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, while also specifically accusing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and then-Defense Minister Yoav Gallant of inciting genocide. "It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the Genocide Convention," Pillay said after the commission's report was released. At the time, Israel dismissed the findings as "distorted and false." MAMDANI DOUBLES DOWN ON ANTI-ISRAEL OCT 7 STATEMENT AFTER BACKLASH Nitsana Darshan-Leitner, president of the Israel-based Shurat HaDin Law Center, cast doubt on the Nobel Committee's decision to award Pillay the peace prize. "A peace prize should honor those who build peace, not those accused of turning Israel into a defendant in a campaign of political delegitimization," said Darshan-Leitner, whose organization has led protest campaigns in Geneva against Pillay. "What peace, exactly, has she brought? The Middle East remains engulfed in conflict, and the region is nowhere near the peace this prize supposedly celebrates." Pillay, 85, was born in South Africa's Natal province to a Tamil Indian family. Her first foray into the legal profession began in 1967, when she founded her own law firm, becoming the first non-white person to do so in her province. GAVIN NEWSOM REGRETS CALLING ISRAEL 'APARTHEID STATE,' BUT SOUNDS ALARM ON 'LEGITIMATE' CONCERN IN REGION During her 28 years as a defense attorney in South Africa, she represented anti-apartheid activists. In 1973, she won a case securing political prisoners on Robben Island, including Nelson Mandela, the right to consult with lawyers. Two decades later, Mandela became president and in 1995, he nominated her to the High Court of South Africa, becoming the first non-white woman to serve there. Her tenure was short-lived because that same year, the United Nations elected her to serve on the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, a body established to adjudicate those responsible for the Rwandan genocide. She was integral in the case against Jean-Paul Akayesu, the mayor of the Rwandan town of Taba, who was found guilty of inciting fellow Hutus to murder, rape and torture thousands of Tutsis. SEN MIKE LEE: TRUMP PROVES AMERICA CAN STAND UP TO A POWER-MAD FOREIGN COURT That ruling set a precedent that rape constituted a crime against humanity and could amount to genocide when committed with the intent to destroy a targeted group. "Rape had always been regarded as one of the spoils of war," Pillay said after the verdict. "Now it is a war crime, no longer a trophy." In 2003, she was chosen to be a judge on the International Criminal Court (ICC), an institution frequently attacked by President Donald Trump as illegitimate. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP After five years on the ICC, Pillay became the UN's High Commissioner for Human Rights in 2008. While in that position, she condemned both Israel and Hamas for their conduct in the 2014 Gaza War, saying both sides likely violated international law. She also condemned the United States for providing funding to Israel's Iron Dome program when "no such protection has been provided to Gazans against the shelling." Pillay currently serves as an ad hoc judge on the International Court of Justice, where she is hearing a case accusing Burma of committing genocide against the Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim minority in the Southeast Asian country.

articles.title: How US midterms could shape 2028 presidential race: Newsom, Vance and other contenders in focus
articles.summary: As political attention turns to the November 3 midterm elections, potential contenders for the 2028 US presidential race are using the campaign season to
articles.body: As political attention turns to the November 3 midterm elections, potential contenders for the 2028 US presidential race are using the campaign season to strengthen their national profiles, raise funds and build relationships with influential party leaders.Several Democratic and Republican leaders have travelled across the country to campaign for candidates in key races, with their efforts likely to influence their own political prospects ahead of the next presidential election, the Associated Press reported.The midterms will offer an early indication of which potential candidates can mobilise voters, raise money and help their parties win competitive races.Newsom, Vance among leaders under spotlightCalifornia Governor Gavin Newsom, who will leave office at the end of the year, has emerged as one of the most active Democrats on the campaign trail. He has campaigned for candidates across several Southern states, including Alabama, Mississippi, North Carolina and South Carolina.His outreach in the South could help him strengthen ties with African American voters, a key constituency within the Democratic Party. Newsom has also used his fundraising network to build relationships with party officials in states such as Nevada and New Hampshire.One of his most significant political bets has been backing California's Proposition 50, which created a new congressional map in response to Republican-led redistricting in Texas. The map could help Democrats win as many as five additional US House seats in California in the November elections.A strong result would allow Newsom to highlight his role in the redistricting battle. However, failing to secure all five potential gains could weaken that argument as he considers his future beyond the governor's office.On the Republican side, Vice President JD Vance's political fortunes are closely linked to the party's performance under President Donald Trump. Vance has maintained an extensive campaign schedule, travelling across the Midwest, the South and Alaska while promoting the administration's efforts to tackle fraud.Ohio will be a particularly important state to watch. Republican Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to Vance's former Senate seat in 2025, faces a challenge from former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown. Meanwhile, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is competing against Democrat Amy Acton in the governor's race.The performance of Turning Point Action, the conservative political organisation led by Erika Kirk, will also be closely watched. Kirk, the widow of its co-founder Charlie Kirk, has endorsed Vance's potential presidential bid, and the group has indicated that it intends to support him.Vance has said his focus is on helping Republicans win the midterms rather than pursuing his own presidential ambitions.Shapiro, Beshear seek to strengthen national standingPennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro has taken a different approach from other potential Democratic presidential contenders, concentrating largely on his home state rather than travelling to early presidential primary states.His strategy reflects Pennsylvania's importance as a competitive state in national elections. Shapiro is expected to win re-election against Republican state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, giving him an opportunity to focus on helping Democrats win control of the state legislature and gain congressional seats.Strong Democratic performances in working-class counties such as Beaver, Luzerne and Erie could help Shapiro make the case that he can win back voters who have shifted towards Republicans during the Trump era.Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear, meanwhile, has used his position as chairman of the Democratic Governors Association to expand his national profile. He is scheduled to lead a get-out-the-vote tour through key states, beginning in Nevada on October 22.Beshear has also travelled to promote his book and meet influential Democrats in states that could play an important role in the 2028 presidential primaries.However, his decisions on campaign spending could carry significant political risks. The governors association has backed Democrats in traditional battlegrounds such as Wisconsin, Michigan and Arizona, while also investing in Republican-leaning states including Ohio and Iowa.Some Democrats have complained that their states need more financial support. Amid the pressure, the association sent $1 million this week to support Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa.Cruz, Pritzker spend heavily on midterm campaignsRepublican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas is also using the midterm campaign season to strengthen his political network as he weighs another presidential run.His Truth and Courage PAC has spent more than $2.4 million on advertisements supporting midterm candidates this year, according to AdImpact, with much of the spending directed towards supporting Senate candidate Ken Paxton in Texas.Cruz has also returned to Iowa, where he won the Republican caucuses during the 2016 presidential primary. He has made three trips to the state and plans to visit Alaska, South Carolina, North Carolina and potentially Michigan.Illinois Governor JB Pritzker, a billionaire Democrat seeking a third term, has directed substantial resources towards helping his party in other states.His team says he has contributed $38 million to Democratic midterm efforts through personal donations and political organisations, including about $20 million through his Ready for the Fight PAC.Pritzker has been particularly active in the Texas governor's race, contributing $1 million this week after an earlier donation of $200,000. He has also appeared at more than 75 events across the country, including in Nevada and New Hampshire, and is expected to visit South Carolina before Election Day.Ocasio-Cortez, Buttigieg test their national appealNew York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has become increasingly open to the possibility of a presidential run, potentially positioning herself as a leading contender among the Democratic Party's progressive wing.For now, she is seeking to demonstrate that progressive politics can succeed in a competitive state such as Michigan. She has backed Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and appeared with him at a fundraiser in New York City this week.“If Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere,” Ocasio-Cortez told the audience, presenting his campaign as a test of the broader progressive movement.A victory for El-Sayed could help her counter concerns about whether her political message can appeal to voters beyond the party's progressive base.Former transportation secretary Pete Buttigieg has also used the period since leaving the Biden administration to campaign extensively for Democrats.According to his team, Buttigieg has endorsed nearly 100 candidates in the current election cycle and campaigned alongside roughly half of them. He has visited 37 states since leaving office.His appearances have ranged from competitive Senate races to state legislative contests and campaigns in heavily Republican areas. He has also helped bring Democratic candidates together at events, including a unity gathering in Michigan following divisive primary contests.As the November 3 elections approach, the results will not determine the 2028 presidential field, but they could help establish which potential contenders emerge with stronger fundraising networks, broader party support and a convincing record of helping their candidates win.You use AI every day. articles.title: Worry not about visa headlines: Former CEO of HCL Technologies Vineet Nayar says Green Card ban on 8 companies is not so big
articles.summary: Former CEO of HCL Technologies Vineet Nayar brushed aside the panic triggered by the Trump administration's suspension of the Green Card process and said
articles.body: Former CEO of HCL Technologies Vineet Nayar brushed aside the panic triggered by the Trump administration's suspension of the Green Card process and said Indian IT companies account for less than 2% of Green Card filings. The direct impact is smaller than it appears. He predicted that it will be America's loss because American companies will now move to India. "Trump may make it harder for Indian engineers to move to American work. The opportunity is to make American work move to Indian engineers," Nayar said."I have spent more than three decades in this industry. So when I read about the latest US action restricting some large technology companies from using PERM, the route through which employees move towards permanent residency, I was less worried than the headlines suggested," he said."One number explains why. Indian IT companies accounted for less than 1,400 of the 117,849 PERM certifications last year. Less than 2%. The direct impact may therefore be smaller than it first appears," he explained.Work in America to onsite-offshore modelNayar said he saw the transition from the time when it was absolutely necessary to send Indian engineers to America for work to a time when it was found that the work could be done from India. The onsite-offshore model was born. This might be the moment of another transition, he said. "America is making it harder to move Indian talent there, while technology is making it easier for smaller teams in India to take responsibility for increasingly sophisticated work. There is an irony here. In trying to reduce the movement of Indian talent to America, the US may accelerate the movement of American work to India," he said."But I don’t mean another wave of coding and maintenance jobs. The opportunity is architecture, product engineering, cybersecurity, AI implementation, industry solutions and eventually ownership of products and IP," he predicted."Indian teams should not merely receive specifications from New York. They should help decide what gets built. Not merely maintain a global bank’s technology platform, but help redesign the bank. Not just supply engineers to solve somebody else’s problem, but own the problem," he said.HCL Technologies is one of the eight companies that got their PERM process suspended.Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu too expressed optimism in the announcement and urged Indians to leave America and instead build India.You use AI every day. articles.title: Israeli settler attacks target Palestinian olive harvest in West Bank
articles.summary: At least 19 settler attacks recorded across territory on Friday as Israeli forces separately detain 16 Palestinians.
articles.body:
Israeli settlers have carried out attacks and pogroms disrupting the Palestinian olive harvest in the West Bank, while Israeli forces separately detained several Palestinians across the occupied territory.

At least 19 settler attacks were recorded on Friday by the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, a Palestinian government body operating under the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO).

The commission said the incidents included attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters, the burning and uprooting of olive trees, and the theft of crops and livestock. Other Palestinians and their vehicles were also targeted.

Settlers set fire to Palestinian-owned groves and stole olives in what is considered the most important season for harvesting the single-seeded stone fruit.

More than 50 olive trees were uprooted by settlers in Qusra, the commission said.

Settlers also assaulted and injured Palestinian farmers involved in the harvest in the Tal, where a Palestinian-owned vehicle was set on fire, it added.

Additionally, olive harvesters were attacked in Jorish, Beita, Naqoura, Birzeit, Deir Bzeih and Farata.

A farmer was injured in reported gunfire in Kafr ad-Dik, and the use of live ammunition was reported during a settler pogrom, backed by Israeli forces, in Deir Ballut.

Elsewhere, an elderly Palestinian woman in Berin, east of Hebron, was injured after settlers set their dogs on farmers while sheep were stolen in Ein Qinya.

A Palestinian man and his child were attacked and their vehicle stolen by settlers in Yabrud. Settler attacks on Palestinian-owned vehicles were also reported in the towns of Sarda and al-Rihan.

Al Jazeera’s Nida Ibrahim reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank said settlers, backed Israeli forces, have grown more brazen in their attacks against Palestinians during the olive harvest despite the presence of foreign activists and observers.

“Palestinians have to go about the harvest in large groups, that include international solidarity activists, to try to stop settler intimidation and attacks,” Ibrahim said, adding that the settlers wait for the groups to start leaving at the end of the harvest, before springing into action.

“It has become a very difficult journey, as the Palestinians try to leave the harvesting areas, Israeli settlers continue to intimidate them under the protection of the Israeli army,” she said.

As Ibrahim reported, a Palestinian family was under attack by Israeli settlers who recently started building an illegal settlement outpost near Ramallah, “using it as a base to attack Palestinians”, she said.

For Palestinians, the olive harvest is supposed to be a joyous season, but instead, they fear settler attacks and intimidation backed by the Israeli forces.

As settler attacks and pogroms continue, the Israeli army arrested 16 Palestinians in raids across the occupied West Bank on Friday, according to the Palestinian Wafa news agency and local sources speaking to the Anadolu news agency.

In Hebron, southern West Bank, Israeli forces arrested nine Palestinians after raiding and searching their homes, including Ibrahimi Mosque Director Moataz Abu Sneineh and Hammam Abu Markhiya, an official responsible for the mosque’s custodians, Wafa reported.

In the city of Qalqilya, Israeli forces arrested five Palestinians during a raid, local sources said.

Two other Palestinians were arrested after Israeli forces raided and searched several homes in Beita, south of Nablus, the sources said.

articles.title: Actor Sebastian Stan asks when did 'conservative' become 'wrong' while defending film against critics
articles.summary: Actor Sebastian Stan defended the "fairly conservative" themes of his new film "Fjord" on "The Daily Show," asking when conservative became so wrong.
articles.body: Actor Sebastian Stan defended the "conservative" reading of his latest film, "Fjord," while promoting the movie on Comedy Central's "The Daily Show" Wednesday night. "Fjord" follows a Romanian Norwegian Christian couple, played by Stan and actress Renate Reinsve, moving to a Norwegian village only to be suspected of abusing their children by what's seen as a progressive nation. The two must then fight to win back custody of their kids from a society suspicious of their traditional methods. Host Michael Kosta remarked that the film could be seen as "fairly conservative" based on its themes of a religious family pushing back against a progressive European country. Stan agreed with the description but said that deeming it "conservative" does not negate the issues covered in the film. 'PROJECT HAIL MARY' WINS RAVE REVIEWS AS ANTI-WOKE HOLLYWOOD BLOCKBUSTER "Some people might characterize the themes of this movie as fairly conservative. What's your response to that? Are people overthinking it?" Kosta asked. "I think that's a pretty fair assessment, but that should not necessarily cancel out the issues that, you know, this family is facing or that the feelings that they have and the desire that they have to, you know, raise the kids in the best way they can," Stan said. "I think there's probably always, right, on either side there needs to be an opening of the door, you know, for a sort of more of a back and forth to happen …. I mean, this is one thing. Like, when did conservative become so wrong?" The Marvel actor added that he did not grow up in a religious home like the family in his film but urged audiences to consider the perspectives of people like the characters he portrays. CHRISTIAN FAMILY TAKES FIGHT TO DC EMBASSY AFTER GOVERNMENT SEIZES DAUGHTERS OVER 'RELIGIOUS EXTREMISM' "As long as there is curiosity at least instead of immediate judgment, maybe there is something else there, but if a family is trying to stay together, we should at least give them the benefit of the doubt, and maybe they are trying to do it for the right reasons," Stan said. Stan also pushed back on critics who accused the film of promoting a "right-wing ideology" during an interview with USA Today published Thursday. "They’re not understanding the nuances," Stan told USA Today. "I find it almost laughable to label it a ‘MAGA film’ when it's essentially about an immigrant family going to a different country and being torn apart. We could change Norway for the United States, and Romania for Mexico, or any number of places where that’s happening." "In America, it’s going right to the heart of this divisive issue that we’re currently having, and the reason people are writing it off or feel it’s a propaganda piece is because we’ve normalized finger-pointing," he continued. "This judgmental, dismissive attitude that plays out online is quite dangerous and naive – but it’s unfortunately predictable in today’s time." Fox News Digital reached out to Stan's representatives for comment. 'MELANIA' FILM LEAVES PREMIERE AUDIENCE 'INSPIRED'; PRODUCER SLAMS MEDIA FOR YEARS OF UNFAIR TREATMENT The film is loosely based on a real 2015 case where Norwegian residents Ruth and Marius Bodnariu had their five children, including one infant, removed from their custody upon the suspicion of abuse as well as their religious background. The family was separated for seven months until they were finally reunited following several court cases in Norway. Though most known for his role in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Stan also portrayed a younger version of President Donald Trump in the 2024 film "The Apprentice." Though Stan has been critical of the president and his actions, he previously defended his choice to portray Trump despite being warned against taking the project. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "There's also a valid argument to be made in terms of, 'Well, I know what happened. I know what kind of guy he is. I see him all the time,'" Stan told Entertainment Weekly in 2024. "Still, I think there is value in normalizing people that we feel strongly about. And people feel very strongly about him in two different extremes: He's either God's son or he's Lucifer incarnate, and I think we need to bring him back down to earth." In a comment to Fox News Digital, NewsBusters managing editor Curtis Houck called Stan's comments "ironic" given his work on "The Apprentice." "It's richly ironic Sebastian Stan would say this after playing a young Donald Trump in an anti-Trump film that the liberal, elitist Hollywood press loved. It must not be so fun for Sebastian now that he's made a movie that isn't as interesting to these same cinephiles," Houck said.

articles.title: Attorney for former Cornell fraternity member wants AG James off case over post supporting accuser
articles.summary: Letitia James posted "We stand with you" days before being named independent prosecutor in the Cornell University Chi Phi sexual assault case.
articles.body: The attorney for one of the former Cornell University Chi Phi fraternity members named in an explosive sex abuse lawsuit is raising questions about the appointment of New York Attorney General Letitia James as an independent prosecutor days after he says the state's top cop publicly took sides in the case before seeing the evidence. "My issue is not political, and it is not personal," attorney Andrew Miltenberg told Fox News. articles.title: At 13, a Nigerian immigrant in Rhode Island became temporarily homeless; years later, he is a neuro ICU nurse at the same state's largest hospital and now mentors future healthcare workers

articles.body: At 13, Usman Badaru arrived in Rhode Island from Nigeria with his father and older sister, expecting a new beginning but knowing little about how to navigate life in a new country. Instead, the family soon found themselves without a permanent home, relying on temporary shelter and help from local organisations. Decades later, Badaru works nights in the neuro ICU at Rhode Island Hospital, caring for critically ill patients and helping young people follow the same path into healthcare that changed his own life, states an online report by 10 WJAR.From uncertainty to a new directionAccording to the online report, Badaru's family settled in Providence after his father chose Rhode Island as their new home. Like many newly arrived families, they had limited knowledge of the systems surrounding housing, education and social services. For a short period, the family stayed at Crossroads, a Rhode Island organisation that provides support to people experiencing homelessness. There was even a brief stretch when they slept in their father's car before moving into family shelter. Assistance from Crossroads eventually helped them secure low-income housing, while other Rhode Island institutions helped the family understand and access opportunities available to them.After spending a year in public school, Badaru enrolled at the Rhode Island Nurses Institute Middle College Charter High School, commonly known as RINI. His older sister had been interested in nursing, and that interest helped spark his own ambition to enter the profession.Finding healthcare at RINIAs per the report, established in 2011, RINI was created with a focused mission to introduce high school students to healthcare careers and give them practical steps towards becoming nurses and other healthcare professionals. For Badaru, the school provided something more valuable than an introduction to the profession. It gave structure to an ambition that might otherwise have remained little more than an idea.Through RINI, he discovered the healthcare field and began taking concrete steps towards a career in nursing. The experience also shaped his desire to eventually help other students find similar opportunities. RINI has since built a substantial alumni network, with more than 700 graduates now working across Rhode Island's healthcare workforce.From student to neuro ICU nurseToday, Badaru has spent three years working at Rhode Island Hospital, the state's largest hospital. He works the night shift in the neuro ICU, caring for patients who require intensive treatment, particularly those dealing with serious neurological illnesses, informs the report by 10 WJAR.His professional credentials include a Bachelor of Science in Nursing, registered nurse certification, Critical Care Registered Nurse certification and advanced emergency medical training. But experience is more than qualifications. His own experience has shaped the way he treats his patients and their families, especially during difficult times. Having experienced uncertainty and vulnerability himself, he brings a personal understanding of the circumstances that can shape people's lives.Giving the next generation a head startFor several years, Badaru has returned to RINI to mentor students, dedicating dozens of hours to helping young people understand the healthcare profession and navigate the steps needed to enter it. His involvement has now grown further. He was recently appointed to the school's 12-member board of directors, giving him a role in shaping the institution that helped launch his own career, informs the report.As a board member, Badaru will contribute to discussions about curriculum, innovation and student support while helping ensure that the education offered reflects the realities of modern healthcare. He will also serve as a bridge between the school and the wider medical community. For RINI, his return represents more than the success of one former student. It demonstrates how education can create a cycle in which opportunity is passed forward.A Trip that Completes the CircleBadaru’s story goes from a homeless teenager to a healthcare professional helping critically ill patients and now a mentor training the next generation of Rhode Island’s healthcare workforce. He remembers the people and institutions who brought stability to his family and gave him a means into nursing. His work with RINI allows him to repay that support in a practical way: by helping students turn ambition into action.Images Courtesy: 10 WJARYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: The internet outrage over Josh Pate's power rating system proves people haven't been paying attention
articles.summary: Josh Pate's JP Poll ranked Florida ahead of Missouri despite the Tigers' blowout win, sparking outrage from fans who misunderstand the system.
articles.body: We are waist deep in the college football season, which means the natives (read: fans) are starting to get a little antsy. Week six is now upon us, and with that, several data points are now available for prognosticators and experts alike to draw from and anger fans with in the process. One man who always has a lot to say is Josh Pate, the college football commentator who started from humble beginnings and is now one of the foremost voices in the sport. JOSH PATE DISCUSSES NEW ESPN SHOW, FOUR FACES OF ESPN, PAT MCAFEE AND FUTURE OF MEDIA COMPANY WITH OUTKICK Pate landed himself in some hot water these past few days for releasing his "JP Poll," a power rating system that goes out every week. A lot of people had an absolute fit that Pate rated Florida ahead of Missouri when the Tigers just beat the Gators' brains in less than seven days earlier. How could that possibly be? Well, if you understood what the JP Poll was, it would make a lot more sense. As Pate explains - seemingly every week - the JP Poll power rates teams based on whether or not they would be favored over another team on a neutral field according to oddsmakers in Vegas. It's a flawed system, sure, but it explains Pate's logic in "rating" Florida ahead of Mizzou. I'm not saying I would pick Florida to beat Missouri if they played tomorrow in the Superdome or something; we all watched that game on Saturday and it got ugly. But if Vegas says that the Gators would be favored against the Tigers, I can't argue with that, I can only use my hard earned money to bet against that. And I would be stupid to do so, given the old adage that "Vegas always knows." So, what do those oddsmakers have to say about a hypothetical matchup between Florida and Missouri? Well, I'm glad you asked. Again, I'm not sure I'd bet money on the Gators winning that matchup, but I'll take Vegas' word for it. PAT MCAFEE HAS OFFICIALLY SURPASSED STEPHEN A SMITH AS THE FACE OF ESPN To add an extra layer of context to things, Pate released his weekly "Commissioner's Poll" a few days later, which is more like the AP Poll in that it ranks teams based on resume and head-to-head matchups, rather than a power rating. And wouldn't you know it, Missouri is ahead of Florida. People have been skewering Pate for his takes this season, and this JP Poll fiasco is just the latest (and loudest) "scandal" of the bunch. But for all the people getting upset about this, it only proves they haven't been paying attention to Josh Pate's football coverage until recently. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE I've been a fan of Pate's show since 2019, when he was a YouTube creator with a mere 20,000 subscribers. To paraphrase Tony Soprano, "I got in on the ground floor." That was seven years ago, and to the best of my memory, Pate has been doing the same thing for all seven of those years. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Granted, the audience has grown and sponsors have been added to the mix, but he's still the same bald guy with the white t-shirt he was all those years ago. This is what happens when you grow your audience but stay the same. You can either change and alienate your core following (think Metallica after "The Black Album") or you can keep doing what your "day one" fans love and risk newer followers getting turned off. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER Credit to Pate for sticking to his guns and not switching up for anyone. He's certainly made some enemies in the past year or so, but from my viewpoint that just means he's doing something right.

articles.title: Two men bailed after security breach at RAF Molesworth
articles.summary: Police say the two Latvian nationals have been bailed with "strict conditions".
articles.body:
Two Latvian men arrested after a fence was breached at a Cambridgeshire RAF base have been bailed.

Ministry of Defence Police (MDP) security patrols at RAF Molesworth, which is used by the US military and Nato for intelligence operations, identified an abandoned vehicle at about 22:00 BST on Wednesday.

The pair, aged 36 and 32 and who live in the UK, were subsequently arrested inside the perimeter a few hours after searches found a small breach of the fence at the site.

Both were taken to a Cambridgeshire police station and have since been bailed with "strict conditions", the Metropolitan Police said.

The force's Counter Terrorism Policing London is investigating.

Its head Cdr Helen Flanagan said: "We're very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites, but there is nothing from our investigation so far to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford last week."

Both men were initially arrested on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and criminal damage - after Cambridgeshire Police officers joined the search - and were taken to a local station.

The Met said officers carried out two searches at addresses in the Peterborough area and that the abandoned vehicle was also recovered by officers.

"A key line of inquiry remains to identify any potential motivation behind why the men were at that location, and this includes whether it may be connected to any criminal activity," Flanagan said.

"Meanwhile, I would encourage the public to remain vigilant and if you see anything of concern, then to contact police."

RAF Molesworth is located west of Huntingdon, close to the border with Northamptonshire.

It is home to the US's intelligence operations centres for Europe and Africa, as well as a Nato intelligence hub. It is not used as a flying station.

articles.title: Peterborough cadet leader posed as girl on Snapchat, court hears
articles.summary: The trial of an Army Cadets leader hears evidence from three alleged teenage victims.
articles.body:
Army cadets who thought they were sharing nude photos with a teenage girl on the messaging app Snapchat were in fact communicating with their instructor, a court has heard.

Rylan Ray, who was a detachment commander for the youth organisation in Cambridgeshire, is on trial accused of 25 sexual offences – many involving children – which he denies.

A jury at Ipswich Crown Court has heard how a Snapchat account purporting to belong to a teenage girl called Chelsea had been linked to the 26 year old from Westgate, Peterborough.

A boy, who was 16 when he was contacted by Chelsea, said the account sent him videos of a female involved in a sex act and that he returned similar videos of himself.

In a police interview played to the jury, the boy said he was "surprised" when the person he was talking to asked for nude photos of him.

Another alleged victim told police Chelsea had added him as a Snapchat contact when he was 14.

"I added her back; we started talking, she sent pictures of herself. It was a girl. She said she lived locally in Peterborough," he said.

He said he could not remember who instigated turning the conversation sexual, but that the messages from Chelsea became "very constant".

The teenager said he became suspicious when he noticed Chelsea would send the same two or three videos on separate occasions, and eventually he blocked the account.

Speaking of Ray as a cadet leader, he said: "He was very strict with safeguarding rules because he was one of the safeguarding officers."

The court previously heard how the IP address linked to Chelsea's Snapchat account was traced back to Ray's home address, and that her profile image had been found on Ray's mobile phone.

Claire Matthews, prosecuting, told the jury videos of both boys involved in a sex act had been found on Ray's devices.

Another complainant told police he had started speaking with Ray on Snapchat when he was either 14 or 15 and that he had felt pressured to send inappropriate photos.

"He was just asking me to see a picture of my penis and he kept going on and on and on and on about it all the time, so I just sent it," he said in an interview played to the court.

He said as well as communicating with Ray directly, he had also been contacted by a Snapchat user called CJ, who he believed was Ray.

Rhodri James, defending, suggested Ray had never asked the teenager for sexual photographs.

The charges against Ray include one count of rape, four of causing or inciting a child to engage in sexual activity, and three of making indecent images of children.

The offending is said to have happened over a six-year period and involves 11 male complainants, many of whom were cadets.

Ray, who denies the charges, is a former Peterborough city councillor and previously held roles at two schools in the city.
